newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Nov 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Nov 15.

text.p: Trans Power's proposals to raise $1.5 billion through an international bond issue will be jeopardised if the two state power generators carry out threats not to pay new national grid charges. ECNZ and Contact Energy are refusing to pay the increased costs Trans Power wants to impose on them for transmitting electricity through its high voltage direct link. The government has made it clear that if the three state-owned enterprises cannot resolve matters it will step in to stop a raft of threatened legal actions. Trans Power launched its latest 30-year bond prospectus on October 17. The prospectus said 50 percent of Trans Power's revenues were covered by negotiated contracts which expired on the commencement of the wholesale electricity market on October 1. Page 1.

Ansett New Zealand's new 100 percent owner News Ltd says the airline is "definitely" not for sale, dismising widespread reports of a Qantas move on the domestic carrier. Chairman Ken Cowley, who is also executive chairman of 50 percent Air New Zealand-owned Ansett Australia and its partner News Ltd, said in Auckland this week he had received no approaches concerning a possible purchase. "And it's not surprising. We didn't acquire Ansett New Zealand to sell it," said Cowley. Page 1.

While Dairy Board officials were briefly arrested in the U.K. butter import row this week, British businesspeople were being told their country has a reputation for applying European Union regulations more strictly than the rest of Europe. The board fell foul of long-standing EU rules which define butter, threatening a product which has captured five percent of the total UK butter market since its introduction in 1991. Gareth Jones, the board's London spokesman, said an inquiry was under way and technical people on both sides would discuss the issue in weeks to come. Meanwhile, the board has moved its technology to a European company which is using local milk to keep up supplies to the market tariff-free. Page 3.

The Commerce Commission wants to extricate itself from the dispute over Telecom's now defunct plan to form a partnership with pay-TV operator Sky. Early next month, Clear will pursue Telecom for court costs in their legal wrangle over Telecom's bid to form the partnership. It is also seeking a judicial review of the commission's clearance of the deal and several other agreements made subsequent to Telecom's attempt to buy 25 percent of Sky. Now the commission has filed an application to have its name struck out of both actions. Page 9.

New Zealand and the European Union have completed a landmark meat inspection agreement that will cut processing costs and ensure free movement of product when the EU introduces stringent new import checks next year. Meat Industry Association executive director Brian Lynch hailed the agreement as a major step toward reducing the industry's $55 million annual meat inspection bill. It accounts for about 12 percent of the cost of processing an export lamb. Page 10.

Political pressures are becoming an increasingly significant factor in the intertwined world of broadcasting, media and telecommunications. While National is for policy status quo, the Alliance, Labour and NZ First all have plans to cut the amount of advertising on state-owned television. They are also concerned about the growing trend toward cross-media ownership. That means TVNZ is a particularly interested spectator as the coalition talks drag on and as Independent Newspapers (INL), controlled by Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation, seeks to buy a sizeable slice of Sky. Page 15.

One of Australia's most spectacular boardroom struggles will come to a head next Tuesday when Brierley Investments chief executive Paul Collins casts a vote that could decide whether contoversial Coles Myer director Solomon Lew remains on the company's board. Page 1.

Yet another challenge is brewing to the complex and intertwined shareholding structure of Otter Gold Mies and petroleum and gas explorer New Zealand Oil and Gas (NZOG) The NZOG management may face stiff questioning at the annual general meeting in Auckland on November 25 from a group of dissident New Zealanders separately holding around five percent of NZOG.

Telecom on Thursday announced its anticipated $1 billion share buyback - the largest repurchase of its kind ever taken in New Zealand. The company said controlling shareholders Bell Atlantic and Ameritech abstained from the boardroom vote approving the buyback, which is expected to begin in February and take place over a year. It will include the repurchase of shares from Bell Atlantic and Ameritech to ensure their combined holding in Telecom does not exceed 49.9 percent. The shares will be bought off-market at a price which will "largely reflect the average" of prices paid on-market, Telecom says. The buyback is aimed at reducing Telecom's average cost of capital and adding to shareholder value, chairman Peter Shirtcliffe says. Page 1.

Trans Power will introduce early warning systems into the new wholesale electricity market next week, following what it is calling two uncomfortably close shaves in its first month of operation. When demand was higher than forecast by power companies on November 2 and October 17, Trans Power found itself eating dangerously into its reserves. The national grid operator says there are not enough safeguards in the system at present to warn generators and customers that there is not enough electricity being bid to keep the lights on should there be sudden problems. Page 2.

Colonial is set to demutualise and become a listed company following last Friday's members' vote. Colonial plans to mail members their share and option entitlements and a prospectus next April. Seventy thousand New Zealanders will become shareholders. Page 4.

A Commerce Commission investigation has forced Air New Zealand to defer the fixed fee for processing it intended slapping on all import and export waybills from Monday. In turn, the airline's decision has stalled some freight forwarders from cashing in on its controversial levy by passing it on to their customers. Exporters of fish, flowers, horticultural products and manufacturuers has been among the fiercest critics. Some branded the charge a tax because there was no way they could avoid paying it. Page 5.

Apple Fields this week put a deadline on its exit from the industry. The Canterbury corporate apple grower says it will "lay waste" to its 670-hectare orcharding estate by the end of the month if the Apple and Pear Board does not allow it to sell its own fruit on world markets. It threatens to sue for damages, alleging the board, in failing to provide a fair hearing of its latest export consent application, will be liable under law. Page 16.
